extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature; dramatists and critics interested in Aristotelian tragic theory and craft of tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for constructing or analyzing tragedy (particularly Aristotelian conception): qualities of the tragic hero (hamartia), the primacy and nature of plot (μῦθος), and the roles of character (ἦθος) and thought (διάνοια).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero: noble yet flawed (ἁμαρτία/hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic protagonist should be noble or elevated in nature but possess a defect or frailty (ἁμαρτία/hamartia) which brings about ruin; the first false step issues in crime and catastrophe, and the beginning is implicit in the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Othello and Oedipus as prominent instances; Macbeth begins with nobility but the taint of ambition (a primal defect) works as a subtle poison. The defect should make the hero sympathetically human — neither 'faultily faultless' nor a consummate villain — so that weakness and strength bring the character 'within the range of our common humanity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia not necessarily mere accident — moral frailty or error
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamartia may be an error, a moral frailty, or a conscious fault; it is not to be reduced merely to an external accident (ἀτύχημα) beyond human control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two general kinds of resulting collision: (1) the individual violates a known right or encroaches on another's sphere, provoking a conflict that culminates in disaster; (2) internal moral forces clash (struggles of conscience, wavering purpose, divided will). The ancient drama often represents unwitting conflicts caused by human blindness or infirmity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between fate-driven and character-driven tragedy ('true tragic collision')
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'true tragic collision' is one in which character and passion determine destiny (moral forces chiefly determine outcome), as opposed to tragedy driven mainly by external fate or irresistible forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if hamartia is read as accidental, a spectacle of man struggling with fate can still be tragic; but Aristotle's preferred, most interesting cases are those where moral character and will play decisive roles in determining destiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ennobling vice or aestheticizing wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should not present vice as aesthetically ennobled such that its inner ugliness is concealed; doing so defeats tragedy's moral purpose of deterring through consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of Corneille: making wicked characters admirable by focusing on grandeur of soul undermines moral truth. Lessing warns that if vice is concealed/ennobled, 'there is an end to all truth, and all moral benefit of tragedy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal (complex/πεπλεγμένη) plot: change of fortune with peripeteia and/or recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal tragedy, technically the 'complex' (πεπλεγμένη), combines a Change of Fortune (μετάβασις) with a Reversal of the Situation (περιπέτεια) or with Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις), or with both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeteia (περιπέτεια) is variously interpreted: as 'reversal of intention' or as a striking change in situation during a scene (series of incidents in which the situation turns). It may include an overruled intention that adds irony of destiny. Scholarly views (Vahlen, Bywater, Dr. Lock) debate precise technical sense; practitioners should aim for a tightly united causal chain so the first act bears weight of tragic outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (μῦθος) is primary — tragedy imitates action not merely men
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Aristotle's six elements, plot (μῦθος) holds the first place: tragedy is an imitation not of men but of action (πρᾶξις) and life, and the end of tragedy is a mode of action, not a mere quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot must constitute the kernel of action the tragedy represents; without action there cannot be a tragedy (though there may be drama without character). Action includes outward deeds and inward processes; plot should encompass both outward fortune and the mental processes that lead to that fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be dramatic — characters must 'do', not just be described
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama requires enacted action (δρᾶν): characters reveal themselves by performing; tragedy is ruined if it relies on ethical monologues or mere description instead of enacted plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substituting long ethical speeches ('ethical monologues') for a constructed plot. The dramatist should show motives and choices through deeds and speech that have causal force in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must reveal inner life through outward turns of fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward turns of fortune (εὐτυχία and δυστυχία) are the medium by which the inner sense of the action — moral purpose, motives, and consequences — is revealed; plot must not be merely external circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although tragedy uses turns of fortune to bring about catastrophe, these should serve to disclose the inward moral and psychological processes that constitute the action's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Éthos (character) and dianoia (thought) as distinct but subsidiary causes of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Character (ἦθος) and thought/intellect (διάνοια) are two distinct elements that together constitute dramatic personhood and determine the quality of action, but they are analytically subordinate to plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ἦθος is the moral element expressing preāi͜rēsis (moral purpose/choice) and is manifested where moral choice appears; διάνοια includes dialectical reasoning, proofs/disproofs, maxims, and the intellectual means by which characters argue and justify actions. In drama, dianoia is primarily embodied in speech; both must be plausible and conform to necessity/probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dianoia should prepare passions (πάθη) and supply rhetorical/dialectical material
rubrics_metrics.description: Dianoia comprises intellectual reflections, the proving/disproving of claims, general maxims about life, and the rhetorical material necessary to produce emotional effects (πάθη) among characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Greek drama is influenced by political and forensic rhetoric, dianoia often appears as argumentative speech that helps scaffold the plot's causal progression and prepares emotional responses like pity, fear, or anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity/probability rule applies to speeches and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of necessity or probability that governs the plot should also apply to the speeches and actions of dramatic persons: actions and λόγοι must be plausible within the play's world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters' speeches and deeds must follow from established motives and be credible; otherwise the unity and causal chain of the plot are compromised. This supports the view that character-drawing should be sufficiently individual to make action intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to heighten pity and fear — union of the pathetic and the terrible
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal tragedy should excite pity and fear in no ordinary combination, heightening these emotions to their fullest under conditions of the most perfect art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a play fails to unite the terrible and the pathetic fully, it is inferior in perfection but may still remain a tragedy. The dramatist's craft is judged by the intensity and authenticity of these emotional responses.
